comments.author: @GreatDominican
comments.text:
During the 22-year Haitian occupation of Santo Domingo (1822–1844), the Haitian government under President Jean-Pierre Boyer abolished slavery, redistributed land, imposed heavy taxes to pay Haiti's indemnity to France, and enacted policies that suppressed traditional Spanish-Dominican institutions and culture.
Because the era spans legal, economic, and cultural changes, its impact is best understood through the major policies enacted by the administration:

Legal and Social Changes

• Abolition of Slavery: One of Boyer's first acts in February 1822 was freeing all enslaved people in the eastern part of the island.
• Land Redistribution: The government confiscated large estates belonging to the Catholic Church, the Spanish crown, and fleeing elites, dividing the land among freedmen, Haitian soldiers, and small farmers to promote agricultural production.
• The Rural Code (1826): Designed to boost exports, this strict labor law effectively bound agricultural workers to plantations, restricting their movement and forcing them to work under military supervision.

Economic and Political Measures

• Heavy Taxation: In 1825, France demanded a massive indemnity of 150 million francs from Haiti in exchange for diplomatic recognition. Boyer imposed heavy taxes on Dominicans to help pay off this debt, causing widespread economic hardship and resentment.
• Political Exclusion: Spanish-speaking elites were largely removed from high government and military positions, which were filled primarily by Haitian officials.
• Military Conscription: Young Dominican men were drafted into the Haitian army, often serving without regular pay and forced to live off the local population.

Cultural and Religious Restrictions

• Suppression of the Catholic Church: Boyer severed ties between the local Catholic clergy and the Vatican, confiscated church property, and stopped paying state salaries to priests, severely weakening an institution central to Dominican identity.
• Language and Education: French was established as the official language of government and courts, replacing Spanish. The University of Santo Domingo was closed, largely because most of its faculty and students had emigrated or been drafted into the military.
• Cultural Bans: Traditional Spanish-Dominican pastimes, such as cockfighting, were restricted or banned, and public celebrations were tightly regulated.

Outcome

While formerly enslaved Dominicans initially welcomed the abolition of slavery, the combination of economic ruin from the French indemnity taxes, forced agricultural labor, and cultural suppression united various sectors of Dominican society. This led to the formation of the secret independence society La Trinitaria by Juan Pablo Duarte and the eventual overthrow of Haitian rule on February 27, 1844.
